\(A = \pi r^{2} = \pi \times \dfrac{100 \times 10^{-4}}{\pi} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)
The awkward-looking radius was chosen precisely so that \(\pi\) cancels. Hence
\(m = NIA = 100 \times 5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-2} = 5\ \mathrm{A\,m^{2}}\)
(II) COUNTER TORQUE. The field makes \(30^{\circ}\) with the NORMAL to the coil, so \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\) may be used directly, with no complementary angle needed:
\(\tau = mB\sin\theta = 5 \times 2{\cdot}0 \times \sin 30^{\circ} = 5 \times 2{\cdot}0 \times 0{\cdot}5\)
\(\tau = 5\ \mathrm{N\,m}\)
Since the coil is to be prevented from turning, the applied counter torque must exactly balance this, so its magnitude is 5 N m.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem:
(i) Derive an expression for the force \(\vec{\mathrm{F}}\) acting on a conductor of length L and area of cross-section A carrying current I and placed in a magnetic field \(\vec{\mathrm{B}}\).
(ii) A part of a wire carrying \(2{\cdot}0\) A current and bent at \(90^\circ\) at two points is placed in a region of uniform magnetic field \(\vec{\mathrm{B}} = -(0{\cdot}50\ \mathrm{T})\ \hat{k}\), as shown in the figure. Calculate the magnitude of the net force acting on the wire.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (ii) says 'as shown in the figure' and the stem gives neither segment length. The drawing shows a coordinate triad with î to the right, ĵ upward and k̂ toward the lower left; a wire carrying 2·0 A enters horizontally from the left, turns down through 90° for a segment marked 20 cm, then turns through 90° again and runs horizontally out to the right. The field region is drawn as a rectangle filled with × symbols and its width is marked 50 cm. Described in full because this is a free-response question with no options to protect. Page idx 28.
rows.solution:
(i) Consider a conductor of length L and cross-section A carrying current I in a field \(\vec{B}\), with n free carriers per unit volume each of charge e.
The total number of carriers in the conductor is \(nAL\), and the total charge they carry is
\(q = nALe\)
Each drifts with velocity \(\vec{v}_{d}\) and so experiences a magnetic force; for the whole conductor,
\(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}_{d} \times \vec{B}) = n(AL)e(\vec{v}_{d} \times \vec{B})\)
Now recognise the current in that expression. The current density is \(\vec{j} = ne\vec{v}_{d}\), and the current is \(I = |ne\vec{v}_{d}|A\), so
\(\vec{F} = \left[\vec{j}(AL)\right] \times \vec{B} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})\)
where \(\vec{L}\) is a vector of magnitude L along the direction of current flow. The force is greatest when the conductor is perpendicular to the field and ZERO when it lies along the field.
(ii) The wire is bent at two points, so it has three segments, but a uniform field makes the calculation far simpler than that suggests: the net force depends only on the VECTOR SUM of the segments, that is on the straight line joining the two ends of the wire inside the field region.
From the figure the wire enters along \(+\hat{i}\), turns and runs 20 cm along \(-\hat{j}\), then turns again and leaves along \(+\hat{i}\). The two horizontal pieces together span the full width of the field region, 50 cm. So
\(\sum \vec{l} = \left(50 \times 10^{-2}\right)\hat{i} - \left(20 \times 10^{-2}\right)\hat{j}\)
With \(I = 2{\cdot}0\) A and \(\vec{B} = -(0{\cdot}50\ \mathrm{T})\hat{k}\), using \(\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}\) and \(\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}\):
\(\vec{F} = I\left(\sum\vec{l} \times \vec{B}\right) = 2{\cdot}0\left[\left(0{\cdot}5\hat{i} - 0{\cdot}2\hat{j}\right) \times \left(-0{\cdot}5\hat{k}\right)\right]\)
\(\vec{F} = 2{\cdot}0\left[0{\cdot}25\hat{j} + 0{\cdot}1\hat{i}\right] = 0{\cdot}2\,\hat{i} + 0{\cdot}5\,\hat{j}\ \mathrm{N}\)
The two components are perpendicular, so the magnitude is
\(F = \sqrt{(0{\cdot}2)^{2} + (0{\cdot}5)^{2}} = \sqrt{0{\cdot}04 + 0{\cdot}25} = \sqrt{0{\cdot}29}\)
\(F \approx 0{\cdot}54\ \mathrm{N}\)
The bends make no difference to the answer: a straight wire joining the same two endpoints would feel exactly the same force, which is the general property of a current-carrying wire in a UNIFORM field.

rows.stem:
(i) A parallel beam of monochromatic light falls normally on a single slit of width ‘a’ and a diffraction pattern is observed on a screen placed at distance D from the slits. Explain :
(I) the formation of maxima and minima in the diffraction pattern, and
(II) why the maxima go on becoming weaker and weaker with its increasing number (n).
(ii) Write any two points of difference between interference pattern due to double-slit and diffraction pattern due to single-slit.
rows.solution:
(i) (I) FORMATION OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA. Treat every point of the wavefront in the slit as a source of secondary wavelets, in Huygens' manner, and add their contributions at each point of the screen.
Straight ahead, all the wavelets have travelled equal distances, arrive in phase and reinforce: this gives the broad CENTRAL MAXIMUM.
Consider now a direction \(\theta\) for which the extra path across the whole width of the slit is exactly one wavelength, \(a\sin\theta = \lambda\). Divide the slit into two halves. For every wavelet in the upper half there is one in the lower half whose path differs by exactly \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\), so the two cancel. The wavelets cancel in PAIRS across the whole slit and a MINIMUM results. The same argument with the slit divided into four, six, and so on gives the general condition
\(a\sin\theta = n\lambda, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
Between these directions the cancellation is incomplete, and where the extra path is an odd number of half wavelengths a residue survives, giving the weak SECONDARY MAXIMA at
\(a\sin\theta = (2n + 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\)
(II) WHY THE MAXIMA WEAKEN WITH n. At the direction of the \(n^{th}\) secondary maximum the slit can be divided into \((2n + 1)\) equal strips, of which \(2n\) cancel in pairs and only ONE is left over to contribute. So the amplitude reaching the screen comes from a fraction \(\dfrac{1}{2n + 1}\) of the slit, and since intensity goes as the square of the amplitude, it falls off roughly as \(\dfrac{1}{(2n+1)^{2}}\). The first secondary maximum is already only about 4% of the central one, and each subsequent one is fainter still.
(ii) TWO DIFFERENCES between the double-slit interference pattern and the single-slit diffraction pattern:
WIDTH: in interference all the fringes are of the SAME width and equally spaced; in diffraction the central maximum is TWICE as wide as any of the others.
INTENSITY: in interference all the bright fringes have essentially the SAME intensity; in diffraction the intensity FALLS OFF sharply away from the centre, each maximum being much fainter than the one before.

rows.stem:
(i) With the help of a ray diagram, describe the construction and working of a compound microscope.
(ii) (I) The real image of an object placed between f and 2f from a convex lens can be seen on a screen placed at the image location. If the screen is removed, is the image still there ? Explain.
(II) Plane and convex mirrors produce virtual images of objects. Can they produce real images under some circumstances ? Explain.
rows.solution:
(i) CONSTRUCTION. A compound microscope has two converging lenses mounted at the ends of a tube: the OBJECTIVE, of very short focal length \(f_{o}\) and small aperture, placed near the object, and the EYEPIECE, of somewhat longer focal length \(f_{e}\), near the eye. The separation between them can be adjusted for focusing.
RAY DIAGRAM. Place the object AB just BEYOND the focus of the objective. Draw two rays from the tip of the object through the objective; they converge to form a real, inverted and MAGNIFIED image A'B' inside the tube. This image lies just within the focal length of the eyepiece, which therefore acts as a simple magnifier and forms a final image A''B'' that is VIRTUAL, inverted with respect to the original object, and still further magnified, at the near point or at infinity. Mark \(f_{o}\), \(f_{e}\), the object, both images and the eye.
WORKING. The magnification is achieved in TWO stages, and that is the whole idea of the instrument: the objective magnifies the object linearly, and the eyepiece then magnifies that intermediate image again. The total magnification is the product,
\(m = m_{o} \times m_{e} = \dfrac{v_{o}}{u_{o}}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\right)\)
so both focal lengths are made SHORT to make m large.
(ii) (I) IS THE IMAGE STILL THERE WITHOUT THE SCREEN? YES. A real image is the place where the refracted rays actually CONVERGE, and they converge there whether or not anything is put in the way. The screen does not create the image; it merely SCATTERS light from that plane in all directions so that the eye can see it from anywhere in the room. Remove the screen and the image still exists in mid-air, and can be seen by placing the eye beyond it in the path of the diverging rays, or caught again by replacing the screen.
(II) CAN PLANE AND CONVEX MIRRORS FORM REAL IMAGES? YES, under one circumstance: when the incident beam is CONVERGING rather than diverging.
For a real object the rays reaching such a mirror always diverge, and plane and convex mirrors can only make them diverge more, so the image is virtual. But if another optical element sends a CONVERGING beam towards the mirror, the rays are already headed for a point behind it; that point is a VIRTUAL OBJECT, and the mirror then brings the reflected rays to a real convergence point in FRONT of itself, forming a real image that can be caught on a screen.
So the familiar statement that these mirrors give only virtual images is a statement about REAL objects, not a law without exception.
